Paraneoplastic “stiff person syndrome”
with metastatic adenocarcinoma and
anti-Ri antibodies
D.J.H. McCabe, MRCPI; N.C. Turner, MRCP; D. Chao, MRCP; A. Leff, MRCP; N.A. Gregson, PhD;
H.J. Womersley, BSc; I. Mak, FRCP; G.D. Perkin, FRCP; and A.H.V. Schapira, FRCP
Abstract—A 43-year-old woman presented with clinical and electrophysiologic features of stiff person syndrome (SPS),
without abdominal or lumbar paraspinal muscle involvement. Investigations revealed metastatic adenocarcinoma of the
lung with positive anti-Ri antibodies. Her clinical condition improved with diazepam, baclofen, tizanidine, and palliative
chemotherapy. Screening for an underlying malignancy and anti-Ri antibodies should be considered in patients with SPS
when clinical presentation is atypical.
NEUROLOGY 2004;62:1402–1404
Stiff person syndrome (SPS), jerking stiff person syn-
drome, stiff limb syndrome, and progressive enceph-
alomyelitis with rigidity may cause muscle rigidity
and spasms in association with EMG evidence of
continuous motor unit activity at rest.
1-3 Patients
with SPS typically have rigidity of the abdominal
and thoracolumbar paraspinal muscles, frequently
associated with a lumbar hyperlordosis, but with less
frequent involvement of the cervical paraspinal or
upper limb muscles.
1,2,4 They do not typically have
signs of brainstem, pyramidal, extrapyramidal, or
lower motor neuron dysfunction, or sphincter or cog-
nitive impairment,
3 although some of these features
may be present in the other three clinical condi-
tions.
2 Most patients with SPS, jerking stiff person,
or stiff limb syndrome do not have an associated
underlying malignancy,
3 whereas progressive en-
cephalomyelitis with rigidity is more likely to be
paraneoplastic in origin.
2,3 Autoantibodies to glu-
tamic acid decarboxylase (GAD), 1,2,5,6 amphiphysin
I,3,6,7 or gephyrin8 may be found, but anti-Ri antibod-
ies have not been described in proven paraneoplastic
SPS to date.
Case history. A 43-year-old right-handed woman had noted
transient pins and needles and generalized upper limb weakness
after waking, 15 months prior to referral to our hospital for fur-
ther investigation. Within 2 weeks of symptom onset, the pares-
thesiae resolved, but the upper limb weakness increased, with
associated increasing stiffness of the arms, neck, and upper tho-
racic region. She developed an upper limb action tremor, with
difficulty lifting objects, and was noted to have reduced arm swing
while walking. The upper limb and neck stiffness gradually in-
creased over the following 9 months, with intermittent painful
posterior cervical and right upper limb muscle spasms that were
not induced by tactile or auditory stimuli. The stiffness and
spasms improved with diazepam therapy. Three months prior to
admission, the patient noted mild dysphagia for solids and a re-
duction in speech volume. Additional case details are available
online (see appendix E-1 at www.neurology.org).
Methods and results. Platelet count was 474 /H1100310
9/L (normal
range 150 to 400), alkaline phosphatase was elevated at 199 IU/L
(normal range 42 to 128), erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 24
mm/hour, and C-reactive protein was 18 IU/L (normal range 0 to
5), with normal creatinine kinase, blood glucose, and routine he-
matologic and biochemical investigations otherwise. Antinuclear
antibody titers were /H110221/100 (speckled pattern), but anti-dsDNA,
-neutrophil cytoplasmic, -SM, -RNP, -Ro, -La, -Jo -1, -Scl -70, and

-thyroid peroxidase antibodies were negative.
Immunohistochemistry studies on acetone-fixed fresh-frozen
sections of Rhesus cerebellum and paraffin sections of
paraformaldehyde-fixed rat spinal cord revealed that the patient’s
serum reacted against central spinal neurons only, consistent
with anti-Ri antibodies (figure 1A). However, there was no stain-
ing of dorsal root ganglion neurons to suggest anti-Hu antibodies,
or of synaptic structures to suggest anti-amphiphysin I antibodies.
Radioactive immunoprecipitation assays against the recombinant
proteins were also negative for anti-GAD and anti-amphiphysin
antibodies. Furthermore, Western blot analysis against human
cerebral cortex was negative for anti-amphiphysin I, anti-Hu, and
anti-Yo antibodies, but was positive for anti-Ri antibodies (figure
1B). The serum also contained immunoglobulin G antibodies reac-
tive against an additional unknown antigen of approximately 130
kD (see figure 1B). Because all other studies were negative, this
130 kD antigen was not considered to be amphiphysin.
Carcinoembryonic antigen levels were elevated at 103.7 /H9262g/L
(normal /H1102110), CA 125 and CA 15-3 were 45 HU/mL (normal /H11021
25), with normal CA 19-9. A chest radiograph and mammogram
were normal. MRI of brain and cervical and thoracic cord were
normal, and CSF examination was normal with negative oligo-

clonal bands and normal cytology. EMG revealed continuous mo-
tor unit activity in the cervical paraspinal muscles, and in
trapezius, infraspinatus, supraspinatus, deltoid, biceps, brachiora-
dialis, and triceps bilaterally consistent with SPS. EMG of exten-
sor digitorum communis and first dorsal interosseus bilaterally,
and sensory and motor nerve conduction studies were normal.
Cross sectional CT scan of thorax showed a 30 /H1100330 mm mass in
the precarinal region, and a 20 mm mass in the right supraclavic-
ular region, but no intrinsic lung abnormality, and CT scans of
abdomen and pelvis were normal.
The patient underwent fine needle aspiration of the right su-
praclavicular lymph node, and cytologic examination revealed dif-
ferentiated metastatic adenocarcinoma of undetermined primary.
A fluorodeoxy-glucose PET (FDG-PET) scan was performed in an
attempt to identify the primary tumor (figure 2A). The distribu-
tion of tracer uptake was considered to be more consistent with
metastatic lung rather than breast adenocarcinoma.
A diagnosis of paraneoplastic atypical SPS in association with
metastatic stage IIIb adenocarcinoma of the lung was made. The
patient was commenced on treatment with tizanidine (2 mg TDS),
in combination with baclofen (5 mg three times a day), diazepam
(8 mg three times a day), tramadol (50 mg four times a day), and
fluoxetine (20 mg daily). Her stiffness and spasms improved, and
a subsequent EMG on this treatment regimen was normal. She
was then treated with palliative carboplatin and gemcitabine che-
motherapy (one cycle every 3 weeks), with a marked improvement
in findings on FDG-PET imaging (figure 2B). The patient declined
consolidation radiotherapy. Clinical assessment over the following
3 months revealed that her dysarthria and dysphagia stabilized,
the upper limb and cervicothoracic muscle stiffness and spasms
improved, and although she was more mobile, she required consid-
erable assistance with activities of daily living. Repeat anti-Ri
antibody screening was positive, but the titer had decreased from
1/5,000 to 1/2,000 (see figure 1B).
Discussion. This patient had clinical and neuro-
physiologic features consistent with SPS in associa-
tion with presumed metastatic adenocarcinoma of
the lung. However, in contrast to patients with SPS
associated with anti-GAD antibodies, she had mild
dysarthria and dysphagia, prominent upper limb
and cervical paraspinal muscle involvement, and
sparing of abdominal and lumbar paraspinal mus-
cles. In addition, there was mild leg spasticity with
flexor plantar responses, suggesting reticulospinal
tract overactivity. The multifocal nature of the disor-
der, in association with brainstem symptoms, and
negative anti-GAD and -amphiphysin I antibodies,
raises the possibility of an evolving progressive en-
cephalomyelitis with rigidity. Previous studies have
suggested that SPS and progressive encephalomyeli-
tis with rigidity share a common underlying patho-
genesis in some cases,

affected patients presenting with progressive en-
cephalomyelitis with rigidity. However, in the ab-
sence of available tissue for histologic examination,
we categorized this patient as an atypical “stiff per-
son” in view of the normal neuroimaging findings,
normal CSF examination, and characteristic EMG
findings. The presence of dysphagia is compatible
with the diagnosis, having previously been reported
in SPS.
9 Leg spasticity has not been reported in SPS,
but transient extensor planar responses were re-
corded in two patients with SPS in association with
anti-GAD antibodies.
1
From a clinical perspective, patients with SPS and
metastatic adenocarcinoma (including this case), 8 or
breast carcinoma with anti-amphiphysin I 6,7 or anti-
GAD antibodies, 6 appear to have more prominent
cervical and upper limb involvement than patients
without evidence of underlying malignancy.
1,2 The
mechanisms responsible for this apparent disparity
in clinical presentation between paraneoplastic and
nonparaneoplastic patients are not understood, and
although these features are not specific,
1,4 an exten-
sive search for an underlying tumor is warranted if
upper limb or cervical paraspinal involvement is
prominent. The use of FDG-PET facilitated localiza-
tion of the potential primary tumor in our patient. It
is of interest that the patient ’s neurologic status sta-
bilized, and subsequently improved, in parallel with
the improvement in the findings on FDG-PET
scanning.
A 57-year-old woman with progressive opsoclonus,
myoclonus, and ataxia, who subsequently developed
asymmetric progressive encephalomyelitis with ri-
gidity, has been previously described.
10 The patient
had anti-Ri antibodies in both serum and CSF, but
was never proven to have an underlying malignancy
despite extensive investigations. To our knowledge,
paraneoplastic SPS is not usually associated with
metastatic lung adenocarcinoma, and anti-Ri anti-
bodies have not been previously described in this
setting. Although the FDG-PET findings suggested
an underlying lung tumor, we cannot completely ex-
clude a coexisting, undiagnosed occult breast neo-
plasm with positive anti-Ri antibodies in this
patient, and paraneoplastic SPS is well recognized in
patients with breast cancer.
6,7 Further work is re-
quired to investigate whether anti-Ri antibodies are
involved in the pathogenesis of the condition, or rep-
resent an immunologic epiphenomenon in response
to exposure of specific antigens by the tumor.

The authors thank Dr. R. Francis for the PET images.
